INEVITABLE DISCLOSURE DOCTRINE IN CALIFORNIA — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Taylor Morgan · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS INEVITABLE DISCLOSURE DOCTRINE INFORMATION SHEET
This Information Sheet describes California case law on the "inevitable disclosure doctrine" -- a trade-secret theory, applied by courts in some other states, under which a former employee's new job can be enjoined based on an inference that the employee will inevitably use the former employer's trade secrets in the new role, without any separate showing that the employee has actually misappropriated, or specifically threatens to misappropriate, those trade secrets. It is prepared by Jordan T. Reyes concerning Acme, Inc.'s trade secret, described as follows: Acme's proprietary customer-pricing algorithm and associated source code, in a situation involving Taylor Morgan's employment with Beta Corp. This Information Sheet describes what California's published appellate decisions say about whether the inevitable disclosure doctrine is recognized as a basis for an injunction in this state, and about the separate, narrower question of when an injunction may still issue based on actual or threatened misappropriation shown by ordinary evidence. It does not itself determine whether any injunction would be granted, denied, or dissolved on any specific set of facts, and it is not a substitute for that case-specific legal determination. This document is also distinct from, and is meant as a companion to, this project's existing Trade Secret Injunctive Relief Standards Information Sheet, which describes the general statutory standards for enjoining trade secret misappropriation under California Civil Code section 3426.2 and the federal Defend Trade Secrets Act; its existing Non-Compete Agreement, Noncompete Void Notification, and Employee Non-Solicitation Agreement documents, which address the separate statutory and contractual limits on noncompetition and non-solicitation covenants under Business and Professions Code section 16600; and its existing Sale-of-Business and Dissolution Noncompete Exceptions Information Sheet, which addresses a different statutory exception to that same section. This document addresses a narrower question those documents do not directly resolve: whether a court may treat a former employee's mere acceptance of a new, competing job -- without more -- as itself a basis for enjoining the employment.

WHAT THE INEVITABLE DISCLOSURE DOCTRINE IS, AND ITS STATUS BEFORE WHYTE V. SCHLAGE LOCK CO.
A California Court of Appeal decision describes the inevitable disclosure doctrine, as advanced by employers and applied in some other jurisdictions, as a basis for a trade-secret-misappropriation injunction that does not depend on proof that a former employee has actually taken or specifically threatens to use a trade secret. Under the doctrine as applied elsewhere, an employee's new job duties are treated as making the employee's reliance on the former employer's trade secret knowledge inevitable, and that inevitability by itself can support enjoining the employee from taking or continuing the new job. Before the California appellate decision described in this document's companion clauses, no published California decision had either accepted or rejected the inevitable disclosure doctrine as a matter of California law -- the question was, as this same decision put it, open.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "The doctrine of inevitable disclosure permits a trade secret owner to prevent a former employee from working for a competitor despite the owner’s failure to prove the employee has taken or threatens to use trade secrets. Under that doctrine, the employee may be enjoined by demonstrating the employee’s new job duties will inevitably cause the employee to rely upon knowledge of the former employer’s trade secrets. No published California decision has accepted or rejected the inevitable disclosure doctrine."
  — Whyte v. Schlage Lock Co., 101 Cal. App. 4th 1443, 1446-1447 (2002) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2260458/whyte-v-schlage-lock-co/)

This clause's single citation is the opinion's own introductory paragraph; it is not independent of the companion clauses below quoting the same opinion's later reasoning and holding, all of which come from this one decision. The decision itself was reviewing a trial court's denial of a preliminary injunction under an abuse-of-discretion standard of review, a procedural posture this document notes but does not analyze further; that posture does not change the fact that the court's rejection of the inevitable disclosure doctrine was announced as a holding of law, not as a case-specific, fact-bound ruling. THE STATUTORY BACKDROP: CALIFORNIA'S ACTUAL-OR-THREATENED-MISAPPROPRIATION STANDARD
California's Uniform Trade Secrets Act authorizes a court to enjoin actual or threatened misappropriation of a trade secret -- a standard that, on the statute's own terms, does not require proof that misappropriation has already occurred, only that it is threatened. When California employers have argued for the inevitable disclosure doctrine, they have done so as an alternative route to an injunction, separate from proving actual or threatened misappropriation under this existing statutory standard, not as an interpretation of that standard. California's Fourth Appellate District has expressly framed an employer's inevitable-disclosure argument in exactly these terms -- as an alternative asserted only because the employer could not otherwise establish actual or threatened misappropriation on the evidence in the record.

WHYTE V. SCHLAGE LOCK CO.: CALIFORNIA REJECTS THE INEVITABLE DISCLOSURE DOCTRINE
In Whyte v. Schlage Lock Co., California's Fourth Appellate District squarely addressed, for the first time in a published California decision, whether to adopt the inevitable disclosure doctrine. The court surveyed decisions from other jurisdictions -- including PepsiCo, Inc. v. Redmond, the federal Seventh Circuit decision the court described as the leading case adopting the doctrine -- and noted that, at the time, a majority of jurisdictions to address the question had adopted some form of it, while two federal district courts sitting in California had already concluded the doctrine was not the law of this state. The California Court of Appeal held that those federal district court decisions did not themselves establish California law, undertook its own independent analysis, and rejected the doctrine outright as a matter of California law and policy.

  — Whyte v. Schlage Lock Co., 101 Cal. App. 4th 1443, 1447 (2002) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2260458/whyte-v-schlage-lock-co/)
  "These federal decisions do not, of course, establish the law of the State of California or bind its courts. We are free to consider the inevitable disclosure doctrine, and we reject it."

THE STATUTORY RATIONALE: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONS CODE SECTION 16600 AND EMPLOYEE MOBILITY
The Whyte court's rejection of the inevitable disclosure doctrine was tied directly to California's general statutory rule voiding contracts that restrain a person from engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business. The court reasoned that because the inevitable disclosure doctrine results in an injunction against employment itself -- not merely an injunction against using a trade secret -- adopting the doctrine would create, after the fact and without the employee's agreement, the practical equivalent of the noncompetition covenant this statute generally voids. The court agreed with reasoning from a federal decision that the doctrine "creates a de facto covenant not to compete," a result the court found in tension with the statute and with California's public policy favoring employee mobility.

WHAT THE REJECTION DOES NOT CHANGE: EXISTING NONCOMPETE LAW AND PROOF OF ACTUAL OR THREATENED MISAPPROPRIATION
The Whyte court was explicit that its rejection of the inevitable disclosure doctrine does not reach, or change, two other things. First, where an agreement already contains a covenant not to compete -- including, in the court's own example, a nonsolicitation clause -- the enforceability, meaning, and scope of that covenant continue to be measured by ordinary California law governing noncompetition agreements, not by the inevitable disclosure doctrine; the doctrine cannot be invoked to expand, alter, or rescue an otherwise unenforceable covenant. Second, and separately, the court's rejection of inevitable disclosure as a doctrine does not mean that a trade secret owner may never obtain an injunction based on a new employment relationship: an owner can still seek an injunction under the state's actual-or-threatened-misappropriation standard, using ordinary direct or circumstantial evidence of actual or threatened misappropriation; what the owner may not do is substitute the inevitable disclosure inference itself for that evidentiary showing.

CENTRAL VALLEY GENERAL HOSPITAL V. SMITH: REJECTING INEVITABLE DISCLOSURE IS NOT REJECTING THREATENED MISAPPROPRIATION
A later California Court of Appeal decision, Central Valley General Hospital v. Smith, addressed an argument that Whyte's rejection of the inevitable disclosure doctrine also barred any injunction based on threatened misappropriation. California's Fifth Appellate District rejected that reading. The court reasoned that the statutory actual-or-threatened-misappropriation standard is a separate legal basis for an injunction from the inevitable disclosure doctrine, that Whyte itself had analyzed whether the evidence showed actual or threatened misappropriation before it went on to separately consider and reject the inevitable disclosure doctrine as an alternative, and that rejecting the doctrine therefore does not mean rejecting threatened misappropriation as an independent, statute-based ground for an injunction. The court held that the principle that threatened misappropriation may be enjoined remains California law notwithstanding Whyte's rejection of inevitable disclosure.

  — Central Valley General Hospital v. Smith, 162 Cal. App. 4th 501, 524-525 (2008) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2291194/central-valley-general-hospital-v-smith/)
  "Thus, regardless of the conceptual basis of the doctrine, our conclusion remains the same—the principle that threatened misappropriation of trade secrets may be enjoined is the law of California despite the rejection of the inevitable disclosure doctrine by California courts."
  — Central Valley General Hospital v. Smith, 162 Cal. App. 4th 501, 525 (2008) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2291194/central-valley-general-hospital-v-smith/)

expectedJSON.body: The Whyte court's rejection of the inevitable disclosure doctrine was tied directly to California's general statutory rule voiding contracts that restrain a person from engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business. The court reasoned that because the inevitable disclosure doctrine results in an injunction against employment itself -- not merely an injunction against using a trade secret -- adopting the doctrine would create, after the fact and without the employee's agreement, the practical equivalent of the noncompetition covenant this statute generally voids. The court agreed with reasoning from a federal decision that the doctrine "creates a de facto covenant not to compete," a result the court found in tension with the statute and with California's public policy favoring employee mobility.

citations.quote: Except as provided in this chapter, every contract by which anyone is restrained from engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business of any kind is to that extent void.
Business and Professions Code section 16600 generally prohibits covenants not to compete, and California public policy strongly favors employee mobility.
We agree the doctrine of inevitable disclosure “creates a de facto covenant not to compete”

expectedJSON.body: The Whyte court was explicit that its rejection of the inevitable disclosure doctrine does not reach, or change, two other things. First, where an agreement already contains a covenant not to compete -- including, in the court's own example, a nonsolicitation clause -- the enforceability, meaning, and scope of that covenant continue to be measured by ordinary California law governing noncompetition agreements, not by the inevitable disclosure doctrine; the doctrine cannot be invoked to expand, alter, or rescue an otherwise unenforceable covenant. Second, and separately, the court's rejection of inevitable disclosure as a doctrine does not mean that a trade secret owner may never obtain an injunction based on a new employment relationship: an owner can still seek an injunction under the state's actual-or-threatened-misappropriation standard, using ordinary direct or circumstantial evidence of actual or threatened misappropriation; what the owner may not do is substitute the inevitable disclosure inference itself for that evidentiary showing.

citations.quote: Lest there be any doubt about our holding, our rejection of the inevitable disclosure doctrine is complete. If a covenant not to compete (which would include, for example, a nonsolicitation clause), is part of the employment agreement, the inevitable disclosure doctrine cannot be invoked to supplement the covenant, alter its meaning, or make an otherwise unenforceable covenant enforceable.

Thus, regardless whether a covenant not to compete is part of the employment agreement, the inevitable disclosure doctrine cannot be used as a substitute for proving actual or threatened misappropriation of trade secrets.

expectedJSON.body: A later California Court of Appeal decision, Central Valley General Hospital v. Smith, addressed an argument that Whyte's rejection of the inevitable disclosure doctrine also barred any injunction based on threatened misappropriation. California's Fifth Appellate District rejected that reading. The court reasoned that the statutory actual-or-threatened-misappropriation standard is a separate legal basis for an injunction from the inevitable disclosure doctrine, that Whyte itself had analyzed whether the evidence showed actual or threatened misappropriation before it went on to separately consider and reject the inevitable disclosure doctrine as an alternative, and that rejecting the doctrine therefore does not mean rejecting threatened misappropriation as an independent, statute-based ground for an injunction. The court held that the principle that threatened misappropriation may be enjoined remains California law notwithstanding Whyte's rejection of inevitable disclosure.

citations.quote: Consequently, we do not equate the rejection of the inevitable disclosure doctrine with a rejection of the principle that threatened misappropriation may be enjoined.

citations.case: Central Valley General Hospital v. Smith
citations.quote: Thus, regardless of the conceptual basis of the doctrine, our conclusion remains the same—the principle that threatened misappropriation of trade secrets may be enjoined is the law of California despite the rejection of the inevitable disclosure doctrine by California courts.
